name: SerenityOS
summary: Free Unix-like operating system written from scratch in modern C++ for desktop computers, combining a graphical aesthetic inspired by the 1990s with advanced security mechanisms and a native web engine.

content.introduction: SerenityOS is a free desktop operating system written entirely from scratch in modern C++. Started in 2018 by the developer Andreas Kling, the project combines a preemptive Unix-like core with the productive ergonomics and the clean graphical identity of the workstations of the late 1990s (Windows 95/NT 4.0 and Classic Mac OS). The project is characterised by a deliberate intention to design the whole software stack internally, from the kernel to the web browser, without resorting to pre-existing third-party libraries.
content.what_is_it: Technically, SerenityOS is not a Linux distribution and does not borrow the code of a historical BSD system. It is a complete system including a preemptive monolithic kernel, a proprietary utility library (AK - Andreas's Kit) replacing the standard STL, a file virtualisation system with a stand-alone Ext2FS driver, a dedicated graphical compositor (WindowServer), an interface toolkit (LibGUI), and a complete web rendering engine (LibWeb/LibJS) at the origin of the cross-platform Ladybird browser.
content.kernel_architecture_and_security: The SerenityOS monolithic kernel manages virtual memory paging, preemptive multithreading, Unix file descriptors and local sockets. On the security side, the system has stood out by integrating process isolation primitives inspired by OpenBSD: the `pledge()` system calls (allowing a process to give up permanently access to certain families of system calls) and `unveil()` (irreversibly restricting the visibility of the file system tree). Modern binary-level protections are added: memory pages protected by `W^X` (Write XOR Execute), memory sections made read-only after initialisation and RELRO tables.
content.graphical_subsystems_windowserver_and_li: The graphical layer of SerenityOS is provided by `WindowServer`, a custom display server and windowed compositor communicating with client applications through shared memory and high-speed Unix sockets. The native `LibGUI` toolkit offers a coherent hierarchy of graphical components (drop-down menus, bevelled toolbars, file trees) based on the 2D vector and matrix rendering library `LibGfx`. The desktop environment offers instant visual smoothness, a multi-screen mode, a spatial window manager and smooth management of customisable graphical themes.
content.native_web_engine_libweb_and_ladybird: One of the major achievements of the project is the internal creation of a complete modern web rendering engine, independent of the web giants (Blink, Gecko, WebKit). The `LibWeb` library implements the CSS box model, the HTML5 parser and a DOM tree whose object lifetime is fully synchronised with the garbage collector of the `LibJS` JavaScript engine. This work allowed SerenityOS to be equipped with a high-performance native graphical browser, before giving birth to the derived cross-platform project **Ladybird**, now supported by an independent foundation.
content.applications_ecosystem_and_hardware_scop: SerenityOS comes with a native software ecosystem of singular richness: text editor with syntax highlighting (TextEditor), image retouching software with layers (PixelPaint), audio player, spreadsheet, PDF document viewer, development environment with debugger (HackStudio) and games (DOOM, Minesweeper). Designed above all to run within the QEMU emulator, SerenityOS can boot on certain real x86 physical hardware configurations (NVMe/AHCI controllers, Intel/Realtek network controllers), but offers no support for contemporary Wi-Fi chips or hardware 3D acceleration for modern GPUs. Development follows a continuous model (rolling release) under the permissive 2-Clause BSD licence.
content.history_and_first_commit: The project repository has its first commit on 10 October 2018; the anniversary page of the site specifies that parts of the code existed before that date and that this commit corresponds to pooling them in a shared repository. Andreas Kling describes the goal as a marriage between the aesthetics of the productivity software of the late 1990s and the accessibility of the Unix systems of the late 2000s. Development continues at a continuous pace, with no numbered versions published on the site.
content.supported_platforms_and_build: The repository README defines SerenityOS as a graphical Unix-like operating system for 64-bit x86, ARM and RISC-V computers. The repository provides build instructions, manual pages and a Ports directory for adapted third-party software. The reference execution environment remains the QEMU emulator; the kernel is monolithic and the native file system is Ext2, with a driver developed within the project.
content.licensing_and_project_model: The code is placed under the 2-clause BSD licence, indicated at the head of the GitHub repository. The project presents itself as community-driven, with a Discord server, online manual pages and contribution instructions in the repository. The Ladybird browser, derived from the LibWeb and LibJS libraries developed for SerenityOS, is now developed as a distinct project with an independent foundation, while the system continues its own development cycle.
content.documentation_and_community: The available documentation consists of the official site (presentation, manual pages, FAQ), the GitHub repository (build instructions, contribution policy, security policy) and the Discord server cited as an exchange channel. The online manual pages document the system calls and the system tools. The site publishes neither a separate release log nor a publication schedule.
content.differences_with_neighbouring_systems: SerenityOS adopts neither the Linux kernel nor the kernel of a BSD: it provides its own monolithic kernel, its C library, its graphical compositor and its web engine. It differs in this from Redox OS, organised around a microkernel with user-space drivers, and from Haiku, which reimplements the BeOS APIs. Unlike Linux distributions, it shares neither the kernel nor the package ecosystem of an existing distribution, which limits the availability of third-party software to the ports made in the repository.
advantages: Operating system entirely developed in modern C++ in a coherent way, from the kernel to the web browser.
Remarkable visual ergonomics and execution speed inspired by the golden age of the desktop systems of the 1990s.
Integration of advanced security and sandboxing mechanisms (`pledge`, `unveil`, W^X, RELRO).
Web engine and JavaScript engine entirely developed internally (LibWeb/LibJS), which gave birth to Ladybird.
Rich ecosystem of integrated and coherent native applications covering office work, graphics and programming.
Permissive free 2-Clause BSD licence and fully public and transparent development.
disadvantages: System designed mainly as a project for enthusiasts and hackers, not intended to replace an industrial production OS.
Restricted physical hardware support (the system runs almost exclusively in the QEMU virtual machine).
No support for modern Wi-Fi wireless protocols and for the hardware 3D graphical acceleration of recent GPUs.
No frozen stable versions: the continuous development model (rolling) can cause occasional regressions.
Incompatibility with closed application ecosystems or native Linux containers.
who_is_it_for: Developers passionate about system programming and C++ architecture wishing to explore a readable and coherent code base.
Nostalgic users of the sober and efficient ergonomics of the desktop graphical interfaces of the late 1990s.
Computer science students and engineers wishing to study the complete construction of a Unix-like system and of a web engine.
Enthusiasts of system emulation and lightweight virtual machines with instant boot.
who_is_it_not_for: General public users looking for a primary operating system for their physical laptop every day.
Professionals depending on recent computer hardware with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth peripherals and dedicated 3D graphics cards.
Administrators of data centre server infrastructures requiring enterprise support guarantees and high availability.
Users requiring a proprietary commercial office suite or enterprise collaborative work tools.
content.verdict: SerenityOS is a Unix-like system developed in C++ by an independent community. It includes a graphical interface with retro aesthetics, isolation mechanisms (`pledge`/`unveil`) and a stand-alone web rendering engine, and serves as an experimentation and learning platform.
content.installation_sur_materiel_et_prerequis_d:
SerenityOS is not distributed as a prebuilt installation image. The installation guide on real hardware states that no such image is published and that a physical installation requires compiling an image from source oneself. The target disk is erased: the guide asks for data to be backed up before any write.

The published hardware requirements are precise: a SATA, NVMe or USB disk of at least 2 GB, an x86-64 processor, at least 256 MB of RAM. Only xHCI and UHCI USB controllers are supported. The system uses the GRUB2 boot loader, which allows multi-boot with another system already installed. The guide notes the absence of real GPU support: neither OpenGL, nor Vulkan, nor accelerated video playback, the display relying on the multiboot framebuffer or on the EFI GOP framebuffer; it also notes the absence of Wi-Fi support.

Compilation requires a recent host compiler, GCC 14 or Clang 17 and later, and a list of dependencies installed beforehand. As an example, the documentation gives for Debian and Ubuntu the command `sudo apt install build-essential cmake curl libmpfr-dev libmpc-dev libgmp-dev e2fsprogs ninja-build qemu-system-gui qemu-system-x86 qemu-utils ccache rsync unzip texinfo libssl-dev zlib1g-dev`, with `fuse2fs` as an option for building images without root privileges.
content.depot_de_ports_et_scripts_de_constructio:
Third-party software for SerenityOS is distributed through a ports tree, and not by a package manager with precompiled binaries. The project FAQ states it clearly: SerenityOS has no Linux-type package manager able to download precompiled software.

Each port is a directory containing a script named `package.sh`, which declares the name and version of the software, its dependencies, the files to download as well as the configuration and compilation options. Installing a port is done by entering its directory and then running `./package.sh`. The `build_all.sh` script, placed at the root of the tree, installs all available ports and accepts the `clean` argument to delete previous build files. The `SERENITY_PORT_DIRS` variable allows pointing to one or more external ports directories, which permits third-party ports outside the official tree.

The build assumes that SerenityOS has already been compiled and that the build environment is available. The ports are therefore not binary packages installable on any system: they are build recipes executed in the project environment, and their update follows the changes of that environment rather than a separate release cycle.
